idiom_name: @Entity with field access, protected no-arg constructor and domain methods
implementation_notes: Java's class model is the pattern's canonical home: private fields, static factories or named constructors, command methods and no public setters; records (Java 16+) make value objects one-liners. With JPA/Hibernate the entity can stay rich by using field access - annotate the field rather than the getter, which is the default when @Id sits on a field - plus a protected no-arg constructor for the provider; the specification itself states that an entity's instance variables must not be directly accessed by a client. Choose the persistence-ignorant variant below when the model must not carry mapping annotations at all.
pitfalls: Access type follows annotation placement: an @Id on a field selects field access and keeps state private, while getter annotations force public accessors back onto the entity - pick one and keep it consistent.
A public no-arg constructor plus setters is exactly what turns entities anemic; keep both protected or package-private.
Lazy loading and proxies need non-final classes and initialised associations; keep equals/hashCode on the business key so proxy identity does not change equality.

variants.name: Persistence-ignorant POJOs with a mapper/repository seam
variants.idiom_name: plain POJOs + Data Mapper/Repository in the infrastructure layer
variants.implementation_notes: The model is plain Java with no JPA imports: private fields, factories and domain methods, while persistence lives behind a repository interface implemented with JPA, JDBC or hand-written mappers in another package. Choose it when the rich model deliberately diverges from the schema (inheritance, strategies, small interconnected objects - Fowler's rich Domain Model), when several contexts share the model, or when annotations in the domain are unacceptable. The cost is that the mapping code is now yours to write and test.
pitfalls: Mapping code is now yours: without an identity map or unit of work, every load creates fresh objects and change tracking has to be made explicit.
Because nothing enforces the mapping, a field rename can silently break persistence - cover the round trip with integration tests.
It is tempting to rebuild a parallel anemic DTO layer next to the model; map directly from rows into domain constructors instead.
